docs.title: A first simulation in five steps
docs.text:
1. Install Scilab 2027 and, on Windows, Visual Studio or the Build Tools with the workload Desktop development with C++.
  2. Clone Stepper-Lab and Stepper-C next to each other.
  3. In Scilab, open start_lab.sce and press F5.
  4. Choose the scenario Velocity step to 1 rev/s and press Run. The first run compiles the library.
  5. Press Report to see the currents, speed, position and load angle.

The same run from a script:

exec("loader.sce", -1);         // from the root of the repository
res = lab_run("SIL", 3);
d = sil_report_data(res);
mprintf("%d samples, %d panels\n", size(res.values, 1), size(d.panels));

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project are documented in this file. The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• sil/c/sstep_plant.c: sin / cos of the electrical angle once per RK4 step instead of in each of the four stages; the stages shift them with the angle addition (Taylor series of the shift, exact to double precision below 0.25 rad, the library above), and sin(4 pe) comes from the double-angle identity. Same equations; one step differs by 1 to 2 ulp. On a Cortex-M4F (the simulated motor of the Doppelstep firmware) the fast loop with the model drops from 47.5 to 37 µs of the 50 µs PWM period during a move.
  • Public name: Stepper-Lab (file banners, window, README).
  • README.md is short; its content moved to the documentation.
  • sil_report: larger figure, legends inside the panels, scales from the run up to shortly after the first fault (ylim of sil_report_data).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• sil_ctrl_dir finds a clone of the public repository, the folder Stepper-C, in ext/ or next to this repository, before the old name sfs-stepper-ctrl.
  • The window: the list of test groups starts on All; buttons look like buttons.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Documentation website (MkDocs Material, mkdocs.yml, docs/, published by .github/workflows/documentation.yml) and PDF manual (tools/docs/build_manual.py), from one set of sources. The version comes from the git tag.
  • tools/docs/export_figures.sce writes the data of the result figures to docs/assets/data/; tools/docs/diagrams.py draws them; tools/docs/check_examples.sce runs the examples of the documentation.
  • stepper_lab (start_lab.sce, xcos/lab_diagram.sci): a model for experiments, beside the unchanged stepper_sil. Superblocks Inputs, Controller, Plant, Outputs; any Xcos source drives the motion command (velocity or position), the run current and the load torque (STEPPER_CTRL_IO, STEPPER_PLANT_IO, STEPPER_MONITOR_IO); inputs out of range are limited, a fault does not end the simulation; five named scopes; sil.values columns 20 to 23; sil_report(sil) (sil_report_data without graphics).
  • MIL (xcos/stepper_lab_mil.zcos, STEPPER_CTRL_MIL): the Scilab prototype in the same layout. model/ctrl_period.sci holds one controller period, which sim_closed_loop calls too, so the algorithm has one implementation.
  • Window (lab_window): library folder, ngspice stage file, backend, MIL or SIL, scenarios (lab_scenarios, lab_run), comparison, tests in a second Scilab process. Settings per user in SCIHOME/sfs_stepper_lab.json (lab_settings_*).
  • Library folder: sil_ctrl_dir also looks in the saved folder, after SSTEP_CTRL_DIR.
  • ngspice stage file: stage_load, stage_active (SSTEP_STAGE_FILE, saved, default); board_bg431b_esc1 and the tests use the active file. tests/run_all.sce prints the library and the stage file, and fails on a selected file that is not valid. X04 computes its reference with the Python twin when another file is active (tools/ref_switching.py --stage --out, SSTEP_PYTHON).
  • SSTEP_TEST_FILTER selects tests in tests/run_all.sce. Tests C01 to C03, S07 to S11, M01.
  • Stall detection of Stepper-C 1.1.0 in the prototype: back-EMF observer (stall_observe, fast loop), decision with the up/down counter and the learned offset at rest (stall_check, slow loop, integer millivolts), constants (stall_init) and status estimates (stall_status), with the equations of the library documentation. sim_closed_loop runs them with the motion generator when c.stall_time_ms > 0 (fourth output sd: fault time, flags, per-period back-EMF estimates and counter); after a fault the outputs are off and the reference frozen, as in the library. Optional overcurrent trip of the library (c.protect = 1).
  • params/ctrl_default.sci: stall_time_ms (0 = off), stall_filter_us 1000, stall_speed 1600, stall_sync_pct 30; protect 0.
  • Averaged stage with the leg voltage error in the prototype (model/bridge_leg_error.sci, brd.leg_error in sim_closed_loop), the algorithm of sstep_plant.c, so that the prototype and the Xcos plant block can be compared on that stage.
  • Tests T13 (prototype) and S06 (Xcos, FIXED and FLOAT backends; the other backend runs S01–S06 in a second Scilab process, tests/run_sil_backend.sce): must trip (stall at the hold current, load step above the pull-out torque, overload at start, blocked rotor), must not trip (enable and run → hold current steps, T05, T07, T09, T08 parameter uncertainty, T11 detent sweep and mid-band), on the averaged stage with the leg voltage error and on the switching stage; the Xcos run equals the prototype including the time of the fault. Scenarios in tests/sim_stall_cases.sci. Results in the README (Stall detection). Must-trip scenarios of a heavy axis and must-not-trip scenarios with heavy load and at the voltage limit, for the changes of the detector in Stepper-C (window on e_d, hold after a reversed back-EMF, stall flag with the overcurrent trip), ported to the prototype. The must-trip verdict asks for SSTEP_FAULT_STALL in the first fault, also with SSTEP_FAULT_OVERCURRENT.
  • sil/c/sstep_plant.[ch]: the plant model (averaged and switching power stage, motor, ADC) in portable C, double or single precision (SSTEP_PLANT_FLOAT), the switching stage optional (SSTEP_PLANT_SWITCHING); outputs off as zero voltage or open windings. Used by the Xcos plant block and by builds for other targets.
  • Averaged stage with the ngspice leg voltage error table (brd.leg_error, stage_esc1_spice().leg_error); test S05 against the switching stage.

  • tools/export_params.py: params/motor_*.json from params/motor_*.sci (--check for CI); params/motor_17hs19_2004s1.json.

  • Averaged two-phase hybrid stepper motor model (model/): state equations [iA; iB; w; theta], back-EMF, torque with optional detent term, viscous friction, locked-rotor option; stepper_simulate() with lsoda.

  • Parameters of the StepperOnline 17HS19-2004S1 (params/motor_17hs19_2004s1.sci).
  • Sources src_dc and src_open_loop (phase voltages and load torque).
  • Tests T00 (conventions), T01 (steady state V/R), T02 (time constant L/R) and X01 (cross-check with the Python twin), runner tests/run_all.sce.
  • Python twin tools/ref_model.py and reference data tests/reference/.
  • Demo demos/demo_open_loop.sce.
  • Discrete current loop (prototype of the Stepper-C fast loop): current_pi_gains, current_pi, current_pi_update (back-calculation anti-windup), one-period computation delay, back-EMF feed-forward, sim_closed_loop with an RK4 plant.
  • Averaged power stage bridge_avg for two H-bridges and for three legs with a common leg (B-G431B-ESC1), voltage vector limited with its direction kept.
  • Parameters board_bg431b_esc1, ctrl_default; references ref_current_step, ref_const_speed.

  • Tests B01 (power stage), T03 (microstepping), T04 (current step), X02 (cross-check of the closed loop with tools/ref_ctrl.py).

  • Motion generator (prototype of the Stepper-C slow loop): motion_init, motion_slow (trapezoidal profile with one-period look-ahead braking, MOVE / RUN / STOP commands, hold current), ref_motion (angle interpolated every fast period); parameters motion_default.

  • Tests T05 (move with speed ramp), T06 (load step, loss of synchronism), T07 (reversal), T09 (voltage limit of both topologies), X03 (cross-check with tools/ref_motion.py).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• stepper_motor_rhs uses the new stepper_motor_f, the single place of the state equations.
  • Reference functions keep a state: [r, st] = ref(t, p, st); sim_closed_loop returns the final state and records the reference angle phi (column 12).
  • Motion generator replaced by the bit-exact twin of the Stepper-C integer algorithm (motion_step, motion_slow, ref_motion, helpers sim_int.sci): exact discrete braking, integer angle interpolation, hold current after periods without motion. tools/ref_motion.py matches src/sstep_motion.c over 3 052 885 periods.
  • T05 and T07 check the limits in the integer units of the library.
  • Software in the loop in Xcos: start_sil.sce compiles Stepper-C (sil_build, FIXED or FLOAT) and opens xcos/stepper_sil.zcos (generated by sil_diagram). Blocks STEPPER_CTRL (the C library), STEPPER_PLANT (averaged power stage, motor, ADC; one period computation delay), STEPPER_MONITOR; computational functions in sil/c/sstep_xcos.c; scenario in the diagram context; results in the variable sil.
  • Board parameters for the SIL model (trip levels, PWM period, ADC scaling); sil_ctrl_rpar, sil_plant_rpar, sil_check_rpar (configuration checked by the library itself).
  • Tests S01–S03: the Xcos diagram against the prototype.
  • Switching power stage (model/bridge_switching.sci, stepper_period_sw): centre-aligned PWM legs, dead time inserted at every turn-on, body diode conduction during the dead time, Rds(on); the motor is integrated between the switching instants. Selected with brd.stage = "switching" in sim_closed_loop (third output: current extremes and mean phase voltages per period) and in the Xcos plant block.
  • Board parameters stage, rds_on, vd, sw_nstep.
  • Python twin tools/ref_switching.py; reference tests/reference/x04_*.csv.
  • Tests T10 (switching stage: ideal switches equal the averaged model, analytic ripple, dead time voltage error, 4 rev/s with dead time), X04 (Scilab vs Python), S04 (Xcos plant with the switching stage vs prototype). Demo demos/demo_switching.sce.
  • ref_speed_ramp (constant current, linear speed ramp).

  • params/stage_esc1_spice.sci / .json: switching stage values generated by the ngspice model (sfs-stepper-power-spice); board_bg431b_esc1 and tools/ref_switching.py use them (effective dead time 133 ns, leg resistance 3.4 mΩ, body diode 0.73 V). New field brd.dead_timer_ns.

  • Dry friction Tc tanh(w / w_c) in the mechanical equation (stepper_motor_f, Python twin, Xcos plant block); motor fields Tc, w_c (default 0, 0.05 rad/s).

  • sim_closed_loop: optional c.mot, the motor the controller is tuned for (gains, feed-forward), different from the plant.
  • ref_angle_step; ref_speed_ramp takes an optional load torque p.TL.
  • Tests T08 (parameter uncertainty), T11 (natural frequency, detent resonance, mid-band instability), T12 (dry friction); Python twin tools/ref_ext.py.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Xcos plant block: 13 discrete states, output 2 adds the largest |iA|, |iB| of the last period; monitor output 5 (variable sil) has 12 columns (+ peaks).
  • sil_plant_rpar adds the dry friction (P_TC, P_WC) and the power stage model parameters (P_STAGE..P_SW_NSTEP).
  • Xcos plant block: thin wrapper of sstep_plant.c; the electrical angle is kept within one turn plus a turn count. sil_plant_rpar adds P_NERR and the leg error table after the load steps.
  • params/stage_esc1_spice.* (generated by sfs-stepper-power-spice) carry the leg error table, its operating point and "format": 1.
  • Controller block: the stall configuration in the parameter vector (C_STALL_MS .. C_STALL_SYNC, C_NPAR = 34), sil_ctrl_rpar takes it from ctl and the controller motor from ctl.mot (as c.mot in the prototype). Controller monitor output 12 values (+ back-EMF d/q, rotor velocity, load angle, detector level); monitor output 5 (variable sil) has 19 columns (+ state, fault flags, the five estimates).
  • test_S01_sil.sce builds the backend of sil_test_backend (default FIXED).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• sil_build: a rebuild compiles every file. The makefile does not follow the headers, so a changed structure with an old object file overwrote memory (S01 to S06 gave nonsense).
  • tests/run_all.sce exits with status 1 on a failure also under WScilex-cli (mode NW).
  • SIL with Stepper-C 1.1.0: make_config() left the new stall_* fields uninitialised, sstep_init() returned SSTEP_ERR_PARAM and S01–S05 failed; the configuration is now zeroed first.
  • SIL build against Stepper-C 1.0.0: the monitor reads the setpoint through sstep_internal.h (the instance is opaque), MSVC compiles with /std:c11 (_Static_assert), gcc with -std=gnu11.
  • sil_ctrl_rpar / sil_plant_rpar with no command or load: Scilab's zeros(0, n) is [], the column check failed.

motor_17hs19_2004s1() holds the example motor. Copy the file for another motor.

Field Value Unit Source R 1.60 Ω Datasheet, ±10 %; older listings give 1.4 Ω. Measure it L 3.0e-3 H Datasheet at 1 kHz, ±20 % I_rated 2.0 A Datasheet Kt 0.2086 N·m/A Derived: 0.59 N·m holding torque, both phases at 2 A. If the datasheet value is for one phase, it is 0.295. Measure the back-EMF Ns 200 Steps/rev 1.8° motor Td 0 N·m Detent torque, not in the datasheet. T11 uses 0.02 as an assumption J 82e-7 kg·m² Datasheet, rotor only B 1e-5 N·m·s/rad Viscous friction, assumption Tc 0 N·m Dry friction, unknown. T12 uses 0.01 w_c 0.05 rad/s Dry friction is smoothed as Tc tanh(w / w_c), so there is no stiction

To measure Kt, spin the shaft with a drill and measure the open-circuit phase voltage amplitude E and the speed w. Then Kt = E / w, in V·s/rad, which equals N·m/A.

docs.title: The Stepper-C folder
docs.text:
sil_ctrl_dir() takes the first of these:

  1. The environment variable SSTEP_CTRL_DIR.
  2. The folder saved by the window. If it is no longer valid, a warning is printed and the search goes on.
  3. ext/Stepper-C, then ../Stepper-C.
  4. ext/sfs-stepper-ctrl, then ../sfs-stepper-ctrl.

A valid folder holds sstep.h, inc/sstep_ctrl.h and src/sstep_ctrl.c. Without one, the error message points to the window. sil_build() prints the folder it uses.

docs.title: The stage file
docs.text:
The stage file carries the results of the ngspice model of a power stage. This project does not start ngspice. To create a file with sfs-stepper-power-spice:

  1. Create an empty folder with a subfolder params, for example my_stage/params.
  2. In sfs-stepper-power-spice, run python tools/run_tests.py --export --sim <path to my_stage>.
  3. In the window, select my_stage/params/stage_esc1_spice.json.

Select that file, and not export/stage_esc1.json, which has no format, vbus or fs and which the window refuses. Do not point --sim at this repository unless you mean to replace its default stage, params/stage_esc1_spice.*.

The active file is the first of:

  1. The environment variable SSTEP_STAGE_FILE.
  2. The file saved by the window.
  3. The default, params/stage_esc1_spice.

Simulations and tests use the active file, and tests/run_all.sce prints it at its start and end. A selected file that is not valid counts as a test failure, so a result never comes from another source without saying so.

Field Check Meaning format Must be 1 Version of the file format vbus, fs One finite number, positive Operating point of the table, V and Hz r_leg One finite number, not negative Leg resistance: switch and shunt, Ω vd The same Body diode voltage, V dead_timer_ns, dead_eff_ns The same Dead time in the timer; effective dead time leg_error_table 1 to 16 rows [i v], finite, current rising Leg voltage error against leg current

The table is valid at its operating point. The window warns when vbus or fs differs from the board.

The default file gives:

Value Result Note Effective dead time 133 ns Timer 500 ns (assumption), minus the turn-off delay of the MOSFET; fitted for 1 to 3 A Leg resistance 3.4 mΩ Switch 1.9 mΩ, with the low-side 3 mΩ shunt (assumption), averaged Body diode 0.73 V At 2 A

Below 1 A the real dead time error is smaller than the model, because the phase current charges the switch node too slowly: 50 % of the model at 0.5 A, and 25 % at 0.25 A.

stg = stage_active();
mprintf("%g V, %g kHz, %d table points\n", stg.vbus, stg.fs / 1000, size(stg.leg_error, 1));

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This chapter takes you from an empty folder to the first simulation in the Lab window. Plan a few minutes, plus the one compilation of the library.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Item Note Scilab 2027 With Xcos. All results in this manual come from 2027.0.0 on Windows 10 C compiler The one Scilab uses for toolboxes. On Windows: Visual Studio or the free Build Tools, with the workload Desktop development with C++. sil_build() also has a gcc path for Linux, which was not run for this manual Stepper-C The sources of the library; only needed once to compile, and again when they change Python 3 with numpy and scipy Optional: the Python twin, and test X04 with another stage file

docs.title: Get the sources
docs.text:
Clone both repositories next to each other. The model then finds the library by itself:

git clone https://github.com/AntonVynohradov/Stepper-Lab.git
git clone https://github.com/AntonVynohradov/Stepper-C.git

The library can also be in any other folder: select it in the window, or see the search order.

docs.title: First run: the Lab window
docs.text:
1. Start Scilab, open start_lab.sce in its editor, and press F5.
  2. Check the first line of the window, Stepper-C library. It shows the folder and OK. If it asks for the folder, press Browse and select it.
  3. Leave SIL: C code selected. Choose the scenario Velocity step to 1 rev/s.
  4. Press Run. The first run compiles the library. The status line at the bottom then says that the run finished.
  5. Press Report. A figure shows currents, speed, position, load angle, voltages and the detector, each with a title, a unit and a legend.

To see the diagram itself, press Open in Xcos, then press Start in Xcos. The Lab Window and Diagrams explains each part.

docs.title: First run: from a script
docs.text:
Everything the window does is available as a function. Load the functions once per Scilab session, from the root of the repository; start_lab.sce and start_sil.sce do it too. The examples in this manual assume that this has been done.

exec("loader.sce", -1);
res = lab_run("SIL", 3);        // scenario 3: velocity step to 1 rev/s
d = sil_report_data(res);       // the panels of the report, and the first fault
mprintf("%d samples, last speed %.0f rpm\n", size(res.values, 1), res.values($, 5));

Results are in res.time and res.values; Reference lists the columns.

docs.title: The original SIL diagram
docs.text: start_sil.sce compiles the library and opens xcos/stepper_sil.zcos, the diagram with the command table as its only input. It is kept unchanged next to the Lab, and its scenario is set under Simulation → Set Context. MIL and SIL describes it.

docs.title: The model without a controller
docs.text:
The motor equations can also be used alone, with a voltage source:

mot = motor_17hs19_2004s1();
srcp = struct("V", 3.2, "f_el", 5, "TL", 0);
t = 0:1e-4:0.04;
x = stepper_simulate(mot, src_open_loop, srcp, t);

demos/demo_open_loop.sce and demos/demo_switching.sce are scripts with plots.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
From the root of the repository, with the bin folder of Scilab in PATH:

WScilex-cli -quit -f tests/run_all.sce      # Windows
scilab-cli -quit -f tests/run_all.sce       # Linux

A full run takes hours, so use the groups of the window or SSTEP_TEST_FILTER for everyday work. Verification has the details.

docs.title: Use your own signal
docs.text:
1. In the window, choose a scenario and press Open in Xcos. This links the library.
  2. Open Simulation → Set Context. A scenario adds its own lines at the end of the context, such as T_end, lab_mode or lab_cmd, and these win over the lines above them. Change your values there.
  3. Open the superblock Inputs and replace the source with, for example, STEP_FUNCTION, GENSIN_f or RAMP.
  4. Press Start. The scopes show the run, and sil holds the results when it ends.

To open xcos/stepper_lab.zcos directly, first run exec("loader.sce", -1); and sil_build("FIXED"); in Scilab. Otherwise the functions of the context and the C blocks are not there, and Start fails.

docs.text:
Input Unit Read Limits Motion command Microsteps/s with lab_mode = 1; microsteps with lab_mode = 2; unused with lab_mode = 0 Once per slow period (1 kHz) Velocity to ±mp.v_max; position to the int32_t range Run current A Once per slow period 1 mA to the smaller of the rated current and the overcurrent trip. The hold current becomes the smaller of hold and run Load torque N·m Input of the plant None. A value that is not finite keeps the last one, without a flag in column 23 lab_mode Motion command Library call in SIL 1 Velocity sstep_run() 2 Position sstep_move_to() 0 The table cmds, [t kind value]: 1 MOVE, 2 RUN, 3 STOP As in the table

Behavior of the command and current inputs:

  • A value is rounded and limited. A NaN keeps the last value. In both cases column 23 of sil.values shows the flag for that slow period.
  • A new value is applied only when it differs from the last one.
  • The motion generator of the library still limits acceleration and speed, so the applied command (column 20) is not the speed of the rotor.
  • After a fault the inputs are ignored, the outputs stay off, and the simulation goes on to T_end.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The diagram writes sil.time and sil.values; the columns are in Reference.

res = lab_run("SIL", 7);        // load step above the pull-out torque
d = sil_report_data(res);
mprintf("%s at %.1f ms\n", d.fault_names, d.t_fault * 1e3);

// no-run
sil_report(res);        // opens a figure

sil_report(sil, visible) draws every group with title, unit, legend and grid, and marks the first fault. The vertical scales come from the run up to shortly after the fault, so what follows it does not hide the rest. sil_report_data(sil) gives the same content as data, without graphics.

docs.text:
Stepper-C has two numeric backends. sil_build(backend) compiles the chosen one into sil/build/fixed or sil/build/float, once, and again when a source file changes.

Backend Numbers For FIXED Q15 MCUs without an FPU FLOAT Single precision MCUs with an FPU

A Scilab session links one backend. To change it, select the other one in the window and restart Scilab. tests/run_all.sce does this by starting a second Scilab process for FLOAT.

docs.title: How close they are
docs.text:
Tests M01 and S01 to S06 compare the modes sample by sample. These are the limits they enforce and the values measured on the final run:

Comparison Limit Measured MIL against SIL, current step, phase currents 5 mA 1.02 mA MIL against SIL, move of 640 microsteps, phase currents 5 mA 1.28 mA MIL against SIL, commanded position 1e-6 microsteps 0 MIL against SIL, load step above pull-out Same fault within 1 ms OVERCURRENT and STALL at 204.9 ms in both

After the rotor slips, the ADC quantization is amplified and the samples diverge, so a comparison of samples after a pull-out means little. The stall tests compare the fault and its time there.

Compare MIL / SIL shows this for any scenario, and reports differences only up to the first fault. From a script:

rs = lab_run("SIL", 1);
rm = lab_run("MIL", 1);
c = lab_compare_data(rs, rm);
mprintf("%s\n", c.panels(1).title);

docs.title: A configuration the library refuses
docs.text:
Stepper-C checks its configuration in sstep_init().

  • In SIL the simulation stops with the message of the library.
  • In MIL the block asks the library the same question at the start. If the answer is no, or if the configuration asks for voltage drive (ctl.drive = 1), which the prototype does not have, the outputs stay off, the state is 3, the fault flags are 16, and the reason is printed. lab_run() raises the reason as an error, so the window shows it. In Xcos no dialog appears and the run reaches T_end, because an error raised in this kind of block at its start ends Scilab 2027.

docs.title: Motor and Control Model
docs.text:
This chapter gives the equations of the plant and of the prototype controller, in the order the code computes them. The plant is implemented twice, in Scilab (model/) and in portable C (sil/c/sstep_plant.c), and the controller prototype follows Stepper-C. Tests compare them.

Rule: a change of the model is made in sstep_plant.c and in the Scilab prototype together, and a change in Stepper-C is ported to the prototype and to the Python twin in the same step.

docs.title: Motor
docs.text:
The state is \(x = [i_A, i_B, \omega, \theta]\) in A, A, rad/s and rad, with \(p = N_s / 4\) electrical turns per mechanical turn.

\[ \begin{aligned} L \frac{di_A}{dt} &= v_A - R\, i_A - e_A, & e_A &= -K_t\, \omega \sin(p\theta) \\ L \frac{di_B}{dt} &= v_B - R\, i_B - e_B, & e_B &= K_t\, \omega \cos(p\theta) \\ J \frac{d\omega}{dt} &= T_e - T_L - T_f \\ T_e &= K_t \left(-i_A \sin(p\theta) + i_B \cos(p\theta)\right) - T_d \sin(4 p\theta) \\ T_f &= B\, \omega + T_c \tanh(\omega / \omega_c) \\ \frac{d\theta}{dt} &= \omega \end{aligned} \]

\(T_d\) is the detent torque, with one period per full step, and \(T_c\) is the dry friction, smoothed below \(\omega_c\), so the model has no stiction. Both are 0 by default, because the datasheet does not give them. The power balance \(e_A i_A + e_B i_B = T_e\, \omega\) holds without detent torque (test T00).

Convention. With \(i_A = I \cos\varphi\) and \(i_B = I \sin\varphi\) the rotor settles at \(p\theta = \varphi\). Increasing \(\varphi\) turns the rotor forward, and phase A leads phase B by 90°. Stepper-C uses the same convention.

docs.title: Current loop
docs.text:
Every fast period \(T_s = 1 / f_s\), ctrl_period() does the following, as the fast loop of Stepper-C:

  1. Sample \(i_A\), \(i_B\).

  2. Compute the references and the back-EMF feed-forward at the commanded speed \(\omega^*\):

    \[ i_A^* = I \cos\varphi, \quad i_B^* = I \sin\varphi, \quad v_{ff} = K_t\, \omega^* \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\varphi \\ \cos\varphi \end{bmatrix} \]

  3. Run one PI controller per phase, with pole-zero cancellation, so the closed loop is of first order with bandwidth \(\omega_c = 2\pi \cdot\) bw_hz:

    \[ v = K_p\, e + \textit{integ} + v_{ff}, \quad K_p = L\, \omega_c, \quad K_i = R\, \omega_c \]

  4. Limit the voltage to what the power stage can give, scaling the vector and keeping its direction (bridge_avg()). With two H-bridges, \(\lvert v_A \rvert, \lvert v_B \rvert \le V_{bus}\). With the shared leg, \(\max(a, b, 0) - \min(a, b, 0) \le 1\) for the duty differences \(a\) and \(b\), which gives a circular amplitude of \(V_{bus} / \sqrt{2}\).

  5. Update the integrator with back-calculation, \(T_t = L / R\):

    \[ \textit{integ} \leftarrow \textit{integ} + K_i T_s\, e + \frac{T_s}{T_t} (v_{sat} - v) \]

  6. The voltage is applied in the next period, the one-period computation delay of the MCU.

  7. The prototype integrates the motor over \(T_s\) with RK4, with ctl.nsub sub-steps.

docs.title: Motion generator
docs.text:
motion_init() and ref_motion() reproduce the integer algorithm of the slow loop of Stepper-C. Positions are in 1/65536 microstep, and velocities in 1/65536 microstep per slow period. The commands are [t kind value]: 1 MOVE target, 2 RUN velocity, 3 STOP, and in the prototype also 4 LOAD torque.

Every slow period:

  • The velocity changes by at most acc when speeding up, or dec when slowing down.

  • A move aims at the largest \(v_{new}\) for which this period's distance \((v + v_{new})/2\) plus the braking distance \(v_{new}^2 / (2\, dec)\) fits into the distance left:

    \[ v_{new} = \frac{-dec + \sqrt{dec^2 + 8\, dec\, \lvert rem \rvert - 4\, dec\, \lvert v \rvert}}{2} \]

    This is exact for the discrete profile: no overshoot, and an exact stop on the target. The last period stops from a velocity at or below 2 dec. - The fast loop advances the electrical angle by a constant increment per period, and it is set again every slow period. One electrical turn is \(2^{32}\), and one microstep is \(2^{30} / M\). - The run current applies while moving, and the hold current after hold_delay without motion.

Test X03 compares this generator with the Python twin.

docs.title: Power stage
docs.text: brd.stage selects the model, in the prototype and in the plant block.

docs.title: Averaged
docs.text:
"avg" is the default: each leg produces its mean voltage, duty × \(V_{bus}\). It is fast and is used by most tests.

With brd.leg_error = stage_active().leg_error every leg also gets the voltage error measured with ngspice against the leg current, linear between the table points. This covers dead time, body diodes and leg resistance, at the speed of the averaged model. The table is valid at its operating point (stg.vbus, stg.fs). The default [] is ideal legs.

docs.title: Switching
docs.text:
"switching" splits every PWM period at the switching instants of the centre-aligned legs, from counter peak to counter peak, which is between two current samples.

  • Every turn-on is delayed by the dead time dead_ns.
  • During the dead time the body diode carries the current, so the leg is at \(-V_d\) or \(V_{bus} + V_d\), depending on the current direction.
  • Conducting switches drop \(R_{ds(on)}\, i\).

It shows the current ripple, the peak current per period and the voltage error of the dead time:

\[ \Delta v = -2\, \mathrm{sign}(i)\, (V_{bus} + 2 V_d)\, \frac{t_d}{T_s} \]

per phase. The current loop removes this in steady state, but it distorts the current near zero crossings. The ripple on a locked phase is

\[ \Delta i_{pp} = (V_{bus} - R I)\, \frac{\lvert v_A \rvert}{V_{bus}}\, \frac{T_s}{2 L} \]

The results are in Measured Results.

docs.title: Stall detection
docs.text:
stall_init(), stall_observe(), stall_check() and stall_status() are the detector of Stepper-C. ctl.stall_time_ms > 0 switches it on, and after the fault the outputs are off and the reference is frozen, as in the library.

Fast loop. The back-EMF comes from the limited voltage. The voltage computed two calls ago is the one applied from sample \(k-1\) to \(k\):

\[ e_k = v_{k-2} - \left(\frac{L}{T_s} + \frac{R}{2}\right) i_k + \left(\frac{L}{T_s} - \frac{R}{2}\right) i_{k-1} \]

It is saturated at \(\pm V_{bus}\), rotated into the commanded frame (\(d\) along the current, \(q\) 90° ahead), and filtered by a first-order low-pass with the time constant stall_filter_us.

Slow loop. In integer millivolts, against the command of the period that just ended, with \(E = \lvert K_e\, \omega \rvert\), sync = stall_sync_pct, and \(e_s\) the back-EMF at stall_speed:

Case The condition is true when In motion, \(\lvert v \rvert \ge\) stall_speed \(\mathrm{sgn}(v)\, e_q < \frac{sync}{100} E\), with \(e_d\) between \(-(E/3 + R I / 10)\) and \(E/3 + 2 R I / 5\): a rotor that does not turn Reversed back-EMF \(\mathrm{sgn}(v)\, e_q < -(E/2 + e_s)\) keeps the condition true for \(N/2\) periods At rest or slow The deviation of \((e_d, e_q - K_e \omega)\) from its running mean, with a time constant of \(N\) periods, is larger than \(e_s\)

An up/down counter rises while the condition is true and falls otherwise. The fault trips at \(N\) = stall_time_ms in slow periods. With ctl.protect = 1, an overcurrent trip while the counter is above zero reports both SSTEP_FAULT_OVERCURRENT and SSTEP_FAULT_STALL.

The results and the limits of the detector are in Measured Results.

The Python twin has no stall detector; the X tests run with detection off.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Stepper-Lab is a Scilab/Xcos model of a two-phase hybrid stepper motor with its power stage and current measurement. It lets you run the control code of Stepper-C against that model on a PC, drive it with any signal, and read the results, before the code reaches hardware.

docs.title: What it does and does not do
docs.text: It does Why Runs the real C code of Stepper-C inside an Xcos diagram (software in the loop, SIL) The code under test is the code that ships: ADC counts in, PWM compare values out Runs a Scilab prototype of the same controller in the same layout (model in the loop, MIL) An algorithm can be changed and studied without compiling it Accepts any Xcos source as motion command, run current or load torque Step, sine, ramp and your own signals use the same three inputs Models the power stage as averaged or switching, with results from ngspice The fast model is enough for most runs; the slow one shows ripple and dead time Checks itself: tests against theory, against a Python twin, and between MIL and SIL Each model is checked by something other than itself It does not Why Replace measurements on your motor Back-EMF constant, friction and detent torque of the example motor are derived or assumed; Configuration marks which Control a real motor It is a simulation; the firmware that uses Stepper-C is a separate matter Include Stepper-C The library has its own repository; you select its folder Run ngspice The window only selects a stage file that sfs-stepper-power-spice has exported Model temperature, saturation or the motor beyond its two-phase equations The equations are in Motor and Control Model

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: Embedded and control engineers who work with stepper motors and want to see what a controller does before the first power-up. No Scilab knowledge is needed for the first runs: the Lab window holds the choices, and the scenarios are ready to run.

docs.title: Related projects
docs.text:
Project Role here Stepper-C The control library under test. Its sources are compiled into the SIL blocks sfs-stepper-power-spice ngspice models of the power stage. Its export is the stage file: leg resistance, diode voltage, effective dead time and the leg voltage error table

Rule of this project: the Scilab model follows the algorithm of the library. A change in Stepper-C is ported to the prototype and to the Python twin in the same step, and the tests show whether they still agree.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Units are SI unless stated. Positions are in microsteps, with 3200 microsteps per revolution at 16 microsteps per full step.
  • Functions are written sil_report(), and files by their path from the repository root.
  • The current vector is iA = I cos(phi), iB = I sin(phi), and the rotor settles at p theta = phi. Increasing phi turns the rotor forward. Stepper-C uses the same convention.

docs.title: The plant in C
docs.text:
sil/c/sstep_plant.[ch] holds the power stage, the motor and the ADC of the plant block in portable C, with no Scilab header. sil/c/sstep_xcos.c only wraps it. Other targets can compile the same file.

Function Purpose sstep_plant_init() Sets up the model: rotor at rest, no current, outputs off. Returns 0, or -1 for an invalid parameter sstep_plant_set_compare() Takes the compare values; they drive the legs in the next period sstep_plant_period() Advances one PWM period, with a load torque sstep_plant_adc_sample() ADC counts of the present state: iA, iB, Vbus sstep_plant_theta() Mechanical rotor angle, unwrapped sstep_plant_leg_error() Leg voltage error of the table at a leg current Build option Default Meaning SSTEP_PLANT_FLOAT 0 1: single precision, for an MCU with an FPU; 0: double, as in Xcos SSTEP_PLANT_SWITCHING 1 0: leaves the switching stage out, so no qsort is needed

stage.off selects what "outputs off" means: SSTEP_PLANT_OFF_ZERO_VOLTAGE, as the prototype and Xcos do, or SSTEP_PLANT_OFF_OPEN, open windings. The electrical angle is kept in [-π, π) with a separate turn count, so a single-precision build does not lose accuracy over long runs.

docs.title: Measured Results
docs.text: This chapter shows what the model says about the example: 17HS19-2004S1, 24 V, 2 A, 20 kHz, 1 kHz current loop bandwidth. "Measured" means measured on the model. These are simulation results, valid as far as the parameters are, and they have not been compared here with a real motor.

docs.title: Current loop
docs.text:
A 0 → 2 A step on a locked rotor, in test T04, gives the same result on both topologies:

Overshoot Rise (90 %) Settling (2 %) Steady error 1.12 % 0.350 ms 0.400 ms 0.009 %

The figure shows the first Lab scenario, a step from 0.5 to 2 A, with both controllers. The two curves lie on top of each other: they differ by at most 1.2 mA in this run, and the ADC step is 1.95 mA.

docs.title: Voltage limit
docs.text:
The current amplitude falls with speed once the bridge reaches its voltage limit. The shared leg reaches it first, because its largest amplitude is \(V_{bus} / \sqrt{2}\).

Speed Two H-bridges Shared leg (B-G431B-ESC1) 4 rev/s 1.97 A 1.97 A 6 rev/s 1.93 A 1.90 A 8 rev/s 1.86 A 1.56 A 10 rev/s 1.46 A 1.02 A

Below the limit the amplitude drops slightly with speed, because the current loop lags the rotating reference.

Higher speeds are left out: from about 11 rev/s on the shared leg the operating point is a limit cycle (see below), so a mean amplitude depends on the time window it is taken over.

docs.title: Resonance
docs.text:
Natural frequency. The rotor on the current vector oscillates at \(\sqrt{p K_t I / J} / 2\pi\), which is 253.8 Hz at 2 A without load. The loop gives 248.1 Hz (test T11).

Low-speed resonance. A detent torque excites it when \(4 p n\) equals the natural frequency, about 1.27 rev/s. With 0.02 N·m, which is an assumption and not a datasheet value, the rotor oscillation peaks at 1.2 rev/s, at 13.6 electrical degrees. Avoid running continuously around this speed, or add load inertia or damping.

Mid-band instability. Below the voltage limit the current loop damps the rotor. Once the bridge limits the voltage the oscillation grows. A higher bus voltage moves this up.

Speed, shared leg, 24 V Oscillation (electrical) Voltage scale 5 rev/s 0.0° 1.00 8 rev/s 1.3° 0.51 11 rev/s 47.6°, a limit cycle 0.30

docs.title: Stall detection
docs.text:
Configuration: ctrl_default() with stall_time_ms = 50. Pull-out means a load angle beyond 90°. Steps lost is the difference between commanded and rotor position at the fault. The values are from the prototype and the C library, on the averaged stage with the ngspice leg error and on the switching stage. Where they differ, the table gives a range.

The figure shows Lab scenario 8: the hold current starts at 500 ms, the rotor slips under 0.12 N·m, the detector level rises to 100 %, and the fault switches the outputs off at 550.0 ms.

Must trip Fault Time After the pull-out Full steps lost 0.12 N·m, run 1.5 A, hold 0.5 A after 500 ms Stall 550.0 ms 48.1 ms 76.4 to 76.7 Blocked rotor, run 1 rev/s from rest Stall 60.0 ms 45.9 ms 10.0 0.5 N·m load step at 1 rev/s Overcurrent and stall 154.9 ms 3.7 ms 13.4 Overload at start: 0.5 N·m, run 1 rev/s Overcurrent and stall 39.5 to 40.3 ms 38 to 39 ms 1298 to 1354 Heavy axis, J ×100, 0.5 N·m at 1 rev/s Stall 212.0 ms 57.6 ms 36.1 Heavy axis, J ×20, 0.5 N·m at 3 rev/s Stall 316.0 ms 61.1 ms 162.9 Must not trip Largest detector level Enable, run → hold 2 → 1 A, plant R +30 %, L −20 % 52 to 54 % Enable, run → hold 1.5 → 0.5 A with 0.07 N·m 6 % 0.30 N·m at ±1 and ±3 rev/s, plant R +30 %, L −20 % 18 % 4 rev/s, plant R +30 %, L −20 %, J ×5, 0.15 N·m 26 % Move of 6400 microsteps; reversal ±4 rev/s; 8 rev/s on both topologies 0 % Detent 0.02 N·m, 0.8 to 1.8 rev/s 0 % Mid-band 5, 8 and 11 rev/s, load angle up to 107°, no step lost 0 % 8 rev/s at 18 V, 9 rev/s at 20 V 0 % 11 rev/s at 24 V, plant L +20 %, load angle up to 149°, no step lost 2 %

The verdict asks for the stall flag in the first fault, also together with the overcurrent flag: a bare rotor torn away by a large load reaches the overcurrent trip before stall_time_ms.

Agreement. The run in Xcos equals the prototype: the same fault within one slow period, and currents within 5 mA while the rotor is synchronous. After a pull-out the free slip amplifies the ADC quantization, and the 11 rev/s limit cycle grows from it, so those cases are compared by their verdict only.

After a fault. The outputs are off, which in the Xcos plant means 0 V on the phases, and the load torque stays as an input. A constant load then keeps accelerating the free rotor without limit, and the simulated currents and speed reach values that mean nothing. Read a result up to the fault.

Limits of the detector:

  • A rotor that stops while the command is below stall_speed is not seen. A rotor blocked at 0.4 rev/s gives no fault and a detector level of 0 % in 0.5 s, while blocked at 1 rev/s it trips at 60.0 ms.
  • A load angle swinging repeatedly beyond about 120° near the voltage limit is reported before a full step is lost. At 11 rev/s and 20 V the fault comes at 250.0 ms, with the rotor 0.83 full steps from the command.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
WScilex-cli -quit -f tests/run_all.sce      # Windows
scilab-cli -quit -f tests/run_all.sce       # Linux

The exit status is 1 when a test fails. The log starts and ends with the library folder and the stage file in use. A full run took 386 minutes.

Task How Run a group from the window Group All, SIL, MIL or Model, then Run tests and Refresh Run selected tests Set SSTEP_TEST_FILTER, a regular expression over the file names; see below Run the second backend run_all.sce starts it by itself, through tests/run_sil_backend.sce

For example, to run C01 and T13:

SSTEP_TEST_FILTER="C01|T13" scilab-cli -quit -f tests/run_all.sce

In PowerShell, first set $env:SSTEP_TEST_FILTER = "C01|T13". A filter that matches no file runs nothing and still reports 0 failure(s), so check that the log lists the tests you expected.

docs.title: Testing another stage file
docs.text:
Select the file in the window, or set SSTEP_STAGE_FILE, and run the tests. Simulations and tests use it, and the log names it.

  • A file that is not valid counts as a failure, and the tests do not fall back to the default silently.
  • Test X04 computes its reference with the Python twin for the active file, which needs SSTEP_PYTHON or a Python in PATH with numpy and scipy. Otherwise it reports SKIP.
  • Tests that compare against numbers from the default stage can fail with a stage of other values. For example, S05 fails when dead time and diode voltage change while the leg error table stays the same, because the averaged and the switching model then describe different stages. Decide whether a failure comes from the new stage values before treating it as a defect.

Selected tests (C0|X04|T10|S01) ran on another stage file. A full run was made only on the default one.

docs.title: Python twin
docs.text:
tools/ holds a separate implementation of parts of the model, in Python with numpy and scipy. It has no stall detector, so the X tests run with detection off.

python tools/ref_model.py                # motor tests
python tools/ref_ctrl.py                 # current loop tests
python tools/ref_motion.py               # motion tests
python tools/ref_switching.py            # switching stage tests
python tools/ref_ext.py                  # T08, T11, T12

Add --write to the first four to regenerate tests/reference/*.csv. With another stage, ref_switching.py --stage <file> --out <file> writes the reference elsewhere.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• Everything above is simulation. The model has not been validated against a measured motor in this manual, and several motor parameters are derived or assumed.
  • All results come from Windows. The Linux path of sil_build() was not run for this manual.
  • M01 does not cover sine inputs or the table mode in MIL.
  • The look of the window and the diagrams has no automatic test.
